source_excerpt: Cirrhosis is the commonest cause, with malignancy, and less frequently cardiac failure and tuberculous peritonitis, being responsible for most other cases.

source_excerpt: Common causes of ascites by the presence or absence of portal hypertension
topic: Ascites - causes classified by portal hypertension
book_has: p338 classifies causes only by mechanism (hydrostatic, oncotic, permeability, leakage, misc). Not found (searched: pseudomyxoma, mesothelioma, Familial Mediterranean, amyloid, sarcoidosis, veno-occlusive in Ch27).
new_contribution: Causes can also be grouped by portal hypertension. With portal hypertension: intrahepatic (cirrhosis, alcoholic hepatitis, active chronic hepatitis, liver failure, veno-occlusive disease, liver tumour, schistosomiasis, sarcoidosis, Budd-Chiari, focal nodular hyperplasia) and extrahepatic (heart failure, pericarditis, portal vein thrombosis). Without portal hypertension: peritoneal (carcinomatosis, mesothelioma, pseudomyxoma, infectious), hypoalbuminaemia (nephrotic syndrome, malnutrition, bowel disease) and mixed (myxoedema, pancreatic/biliary ascites, amyloidosis, familial Mediterranean fever, granulomatous disease).
reason: Alternative clinically useful classification absent from book; complements SAAG table.

source_excerpt: Renin acts on the basic substrate angiotensinogen made in the liver to form the decapeptide angiotensin I.
book_has: Not found (searched: juxtaglomerular, macula densa, angiotensinogen, ACE in book1/book2). Book names RAAS activation only (p339, p346).
new_contribution: Renin (from juxtaglomerular cells of the afferent arteriole) converts liver-made angiotensinogen to angiotensin I; ACE (mainly pulmonary endothelium) converts it to angiotensin II, a potent pressor that also stimulates aldosterone from the zona glomerulosa. Renin release is governed by juxtaglomerular cells (pressure transducers sensing renal perfusion), macula densa cells (chemoreceptors sensing distal Na/Cl load) and sympathetic beta-receptors (upright posture).
reason: Physiology basis for underfill theory/HRS; absent from book. Reviewer may judge it out of scope for a clinical GI book.

source_excerpt: It is divided into diuretic - resistant (ascites is not mobilized despite maximal diuretic dosage) and diuretic - intractable ascites

new_contribution: Refractory ascites cannot be mobilised or prevented from recurring by medical therapy. It is subdivided into diuretic-resistant (not mobilised despite maximal diuretic dosage) and diuretic-intractable (diuretic-induced complications preclude an effective dose). It occurs in 10-20% of patients with ascites.

source_excerpt: The procedure involves the daily removal of 4 to 6 L of ascitic fluid until the abdomen is completely evacuated

Albumin also prevents post-paracentesis circulatory dysfunction.

source_excerpt: The infection is blood-borne and in 90% monomicrobial. In cirrhotic patients, bacterial overgrowth and small intestinal dysmotility may contribute.
book_has: p343: 'monomicrobial (single organism), E-coli, pneumococci, Klebsiella and gram-positive'; decreased opsonins, abnormal neutrophils. Not found in Ch27: 90%, overgrowth, dysmotility, mesenteric lymph nodes, reticulo-endothelial, anaerobic, polymicrobial.
new_contribution: SBP is monomicrobial in 90%; small-bowel bacterial overgrowth and dysmotility promote translocation of gut bacteria to mesenteric lymph nodes, and reticulo-endothelial function is impaired. Infection with more than one organism suggests paracentesis-related infection; anaerobic infection is rare.
reason: Materially more specific than book; polymicrobial/anaerobic clues are practically useful.

source_excerpt: Bacterascites ... Good opsonic activity -> Resolution ... Intermediate-poor opsonic activity -> SBP
book_has: No figure in book (p343 viewed). Not found: bacterascites, opsonic activity, portosystemic shunt/RES pathway.
new_contribution: Gut bacteria (overgrowth, altered permeability, translocation) reach the systemic circulation via mesenteric lymph nodes or the portal vein (bypassing liver RES through portosystemic shunts); reduced RES and complement activity allow bacteraemia and bacterascites, which resolves if ascitic opsonic activity is good but progresses to SBP if opsonic activity is intermediate-poor.

SBP patients are at particular risk of renal complications (related to systemic vascular changes), which is why albumin is added.

new_contribution: HRS is progressive; the kidneys are anatomically and histologically normal and capable of normal function (the defect is altered renal blood flow). Most patients have decompensated cirrhosis with tense ascites, and the haemodynamic changes result from decreased effective blood volume and increased sympathetic tone.

Figure chain: portal hypertension -> splanchnic vasodilatation -> central arterial hypovolaemia -> sympathetic/RAAS/ADH activation -> intrarenal vasoconstrictors up and vasodilators down -> progressive renal vasoconstriction -> HRS.

new_contribution: HRS prevention: avoid intravascular volume depletion (diuretics, lactulose, GI bleeding, large-volume paracentesis without volume repletion); use nephrotoxins (ACEIs, ARBs, NSAIDs, antibiotics) judiciously; diagnose and treat infections promptly with SBP prophylaxis; pentoxifylline for severe alcoholic hepatitis; prevent variceal bleeding.

source_excerpt: IV albumin - bolus of 1 g/kg/day on presentation (maximum dose, 100 g daily). Continue at dose of 20-60 g daily ... central venous pressure between 10 and 15 cm H2O
book_has: p347: albumin 20% at 20-40 g/day; midodrine+octreotide named without doses; noradrenaline named without dose; no treatment duration. Not found: 100 g, 10-15 cm H2O, midodrine/octreotide/norepinephrine doses, 2 weeks.
new_contribution: Treatment of HRS: stop nephrotoxic agents (incl. diuretics), treat infection; IV albumin 1 g/kg/day bolus (max 100 g) then 20-60 g/day to keep CVP 10-15 cmH2O; midodrine 2.5-5 mg orally tds up to 15 mg tds (target MAP rise >=15 mmHg) with octreotide 100 ug SC tds up to 200 ug tds (or 25 ug IV bolus then 25 ug/h); or norepinephrine 0.1-0.7 ug/kg/min IV, increased by 0.05 every 4 h to MAP rise >=10 mmHg. Vasopressor treatment is generally continued for up to 2 weeks until HRS reversal or transplant; evaluate for liver transplantation.
reason: Dosing detail absent. Albumin maintenance range differs from book text (see discrepancy row).
